title: The rigidity of the Turing degrees
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: An exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) that the partial order of the Turing degrees has no automorphism other than the identity, from one theorem of the literature that is stated as a named hypothesis and not proved here: by Slaman and Woodin, every automorphism of the Turing degrees is represented by a Borel function on the sets of natural numbers. The first lesson defines computability relative to a set through computably enumerable sets of triples, and proves what the course uses: composition, joins, countable degrees, the uniform computation of a sequence that is computed step by step, and the coding of real numbers by cuts. The second lesson proves the category tools: Baire's theorem in the line and the plane, the continuity of a Borel function on a comeager set, the Borel index function of the reductions for sums, and the avoidance lemma (a set that is not computable from A is computable from A and the cuts of u and v only for a meager set of pairs). The third lesson proves the recovery theorem: for a Borel function F on the reals with countable fibres and F(x+y) computable from F(x) and F(y), an irrational t is computable from four values of F at rational combinations of t and two auxiliary numbers, for a comeager set of pairs; the proof is a walk that is kept bounded by one bit of F. The fourth lesson derives that an automorphism with a Borel representation moves no degree downwards (without a hypothesis), and the rigidity theorem from the hypothesis.
prerequisites: core course Mathematical Logic, Set Theory, and Computability (C80): computable functions, computable and computably enumerable sets, the list W_e of the computably enumerable sets (Open Logic Project, chapter Computability Theory)
core course Measure and Integration (D10): Borel sets; the topology of the line and the plane
the lessons prove every other fact they use, except the named hypothesis (SW) of the fourth lesson

checks.reading: The manuscript 'Rigidity of the Turing degrees' (OpenAI, 24 Sep 2026; five sections, 10 pages, 34 KB of TeX) was read in full on 13 Oct 2026, and every step of its own argument was derived again while the four lessons were written: the cuts and their degrees; continuity on a comeager set; the avoidance lemma; the lift of a representation to the real line (Borel, countable fibres, the relation for sums); the recovery from four values (the Borel least-index function, the comeager set of pairs as a countable intersection of preimages under homeomorphisms of the plane and of products, the two fixed reductions near a pair, the choice of the two ends and of the bit by countable fibres and continuity, the bounded walk, the computation of the walk from the four values, the bound 1/(N delta)); the proof of rigidity with its two applications of the hypothesis. No error found. The external theorem was compared with T. A. Slaman's survey 'Global properties of the Turing degrees and the Turing jump' (author's version on the author's university page; Definition 4.20, Corollary 4.25, Theorem 4.29): the manuscript quotes it correctly, in the form that holds for every set. The theorem itself was NOT checked; its proofs are in an unpublished manuscript of Slaman and Woodin and use forcing. Differences of presentation, none a correction: reductions are computably enumerable sets of triples in place of oracle machines, and the manuscript's 'effective substitution of oracle subroutines' is the iteration lemma of the first lesson; in the avoidance lemma the pairs need not be irrational, because a string that is an initial segment of the cut of a point of an open interval is one on a nonempty open subinterval, so pairs with a rational coordinate need no separate treatment; the manuscript's extra requirement 3 delta < b_+ - b_- is not used; the fourth lesson separates the statement that needs no hypothesis (Theorem 3.1). Checked by the program plan/checks_20261013/rt_check_walk.py (the bounded walk with arbitrary bits between the ends in exact arithmetic; the exercise values; the two additions and the inverses of the two maps of the plane).

open_obligations: Named hypothesis (SW) of the fourth lesson: every automorphism of the Turing degrees is represented by a Borel function on the sets of natural numbers, with the equation for every set (Slaman and Woodin; stated in Slaman's survey, Corollary 4.25 and Theorem 4.29; proofs in an unpublished manuscript of 2005). Not proved in the course and not checked. The rigidity theorem of the course depends on it entirely. The programme has no course on forcing or on the Slaman-Woodin analysis of automorphisms.

The course defines 'B is computable from A' by computably enumerable sets of triples. That this relation is the Turing reducibility of the literature (machines with oracles) is explained in one paragraph of the first lesson and not proved in the course. The proofs of the course do not use it; the hypothesis (SW) is a statement about the relation of the literature.

Three facts about computably enumerable sets are taken from the text of core course C80 (Open Logic Project, chapter Computability Theory): the characterization by an existential quantifier over a computable relation, the list W_e with a computably enumerable membership relation, and 'computable iff the set and its complement are computably enumerable'. The lessons use informal descriptions of certificates to show that sets of triples are computably enumerable.

Not proved in the course: the corollary on bi-interpretability with second order arithmetic (the equivalence with rigidity is a theorem of Slaman and Woodin; Slaman's survey, Theorem 5.9). Relayed and not checked: the statements about earlier results (fixed cone above the double jump).

The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader. Because the theorem is a well-known open problem and the argument is short, a check by a second reader is especially desirable here.
